threat_assessment:
Let's talk about how the table sees you, because ten Game Changers sit on your bracket report, the floor is 4, and a professional table's read hierarchy is exact. Rhystic Study on turn 2 is priced in — groans, not removal. Smothering Tithe gets answered on sight. The top of the list is Aetherflux Reservoir next to Hullbreaker Horror: anyone who has done the reading does stack 006's math on sight — mana-neutral loop, triangular life gain, three 50-point activations, dead table — and every removal spell and counter in the pod turns toward you that instant.

So the Reservoir is a sandbag card by default: the LAST piece you deploy, on the commit turn itself, never a turn early to 'develop.' Sol Ring and Arcane Signet are furniture. Hullbreaker reads as a flash fatty and a soft counterspell. None of the three telegraphs the kill — the Reservoir does.

Enlightened Tutor is your scheduler, and it works at instant speed: fire it on the end step of the opponent to your right, your draw step delivers the fourth piece, and the commit turn opens with Grand Abolisher having never shown the table a three-of-four board. The same play is a tell in reverse — a late-game, end-step Enlightened Tutor from a deck with a known Reservoir kill reads as 'the go turn is their untap.' So spend it on the information schedule you choose. Early, it reads as value: a punisher, a tax piece, a doubler. Late and at an end step, it reads as the kill — so do that version behind untapped counter mana, or on a turn when nothing on your board looks like three-of-four.

Telegraph the Reservoir deliberately in exactly one situation: the punisher clock is already public (stack 003's upkeep arithmetic on board) and you hold free counters. Then a visible Reservoir soaks the artifact removal that would otherwise dismantle Iron Maiden or the Mine layer, and the archenemy mantle freezes a table whose upkeeps are bleeding (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection, strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock). That is embracing the threat on your terms. Every other early Reservoir is donating information.

The commit turn is the deck's central play skill, and the sequencing rule is strict: Grand Abolisher is cast ON the commit turn, as its first spell — not the turn before. The strategic frame allows 'Abolisher the turn before'; disagree at this tier. A telegraphed Abolisher sitting through a full rotation is removal bait and an announcement — a professional table reads it as 'the combo is next turn' and answers it, or you, at sorcery speed with three players' worth of resources.

Cast first on the go turn, Abolisher does triple duty. His static closes every priority window for the rest of your turn. He is cast #1 toward the ledger, because Aetherflux counts every spell you've cast this turn — your setup spells are already storm count. And the only interactable moment left is the response window to Abolisher himself, while the expensive pieces are still safe in hand.

Be honest about the windows, because stack 006 is. Without Abolisher, all 15 casts and all three activations pass priority to every opponent; activating is not casting, so Hullbreaker never triggers in those windows, and the sorcery-speed loop pieces give you zero mid-stack plays. What punishes you there is instant-speed only: a counterspell on a loop rock, artifact removal on any piece mid-ledger, a protection effect on the seat you targeted, and above all a damage-redirect effect on an activation — the verified ledger has you at 3 life after the first payment, so a Deflecting Swat-class response kills YOU with your own Reservoir.

Under Abolisher the residual outs shrink to land-channel effects — Otawara and Boseiju are land cards, outside 'artifacts, creatures, or enchantments' — and to the interrupts that never needed a window at all: cast-limit and cast-tax statics already on the battlefield. A Rule of Law-class effect ends a 15-cast line outright; a Thalia- or Trinisphere-class tax breaks the loop's verified mana-neutrality (stacks 004/005). Scan the table for those BEFORE you go. They beat Abolisher because they are not responses (strategy:critical-mass.storm-math, strategy:pivot-point).

Drannith Magistrate carries its own political mass — one of the ten names on the bracket report, and the table treats it that way. Cast turn 2 into a fresh pod, it unites three commander-dependent players against you for no immediate return. Cast when one commander is the table's shared problem, it is coalition glue two opponents will actively protect (strategy:multiplayer.politics). Treat it as both a magnet and a bargaining chip — and know its stranding ceiling (Drannith plus Verdict or Path locking a commander out of the zone-replacement recast) is an unverified candidate: do not promise the table, or yourself, a line no stack has passed.

The walker layer is four deep, and it changes your flip-point math in the long game: Jace Beleren, Jace, Wielder of Mysteries, Teferi, Temporal Pilgrim, and Teferi, Hero of Dominaria all survive Supreme Verdict in BOTH directions. Hero of Dominaria dissolves the draw-go deck's oldest tension with one permanent — his +1 draws a card AND untaps two lands at the next end step, so you advance a clock that survives your own wraths while your Counterspell mana never closes (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math). Beleren's +2 reads as a gift while feeding Heliod's discount and the punisher thresholds off all three opponents' draws.

Know your flip points — the moments the table stops ignoring you. One: engine plus punisher both visible; the stack 003 clock assembles by turn 6 in 41.2% of games (56.7% ever, mean turn 4.215). Two: Forced Fruition resolving — the loudest card in the deck. Three: Heliod flipped with cards in hand; your untapped mana is read as interaction forever after (commander mean cast 4.133, 90.2% by turn 6). Four: the Reservoir next to Hullbreaker — the loudest of all. Five: any end-step Enlightened Tutor past the midgame.

Your closing speed backs the posture: wincon access is 50.5% by turn 6 and 61.2% ever, so 'stay small, stay boring' has an expiry date. The moment Enlightened Tutor schedules the fourth piece behind an Abolisher, stop playing fair (strategy:pivot-point).
matchups:
Sweeper control and the control mirror: someone must be the beatdown, and it is not you. The stack 003 punisher clock advances while both of you draw-go, so you own the long game (strategy:whos-the-beatdown, strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock). Your board is sweep-layered four walkers deep — Beleren, Wielder of Mysteries, Temporal Pilgrim, and Teferi, Hero of Dominaria all live through every Supreme Verdict, including YOURS. Wrath their Torrential Gearhulk board through open permission (it can't be countered) while the walkers keep drawing: that is resilience bought instead of restraint (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math).

Hero of Dominaria is the mirror's best card. The +1 draws and untaps two lands at the next end step, so your clock ticks while {U}{U} stays open — the mirror's central dilemma, deleted — and the -3 tucks the one permanent their deck can't easily rebuy. Archmage's Charm is the other mirror card: in a permission stalemate the draw-two mode means your held interaction is never dead, and stealing an opposing Sol Ring at mana value 1 is real tempo in a rock-driven matchup.

Creature wraths hit almost nothing of yours (mean 1.513 bodies by turn 6 in the goldfish) — with one big exception: Hullbreaker Horror. It is a combo piece first and a blocker never. Do not flash it in early as value into a control seat; a wrath that takes it costs you the verified kill, not a 7-drop.

Your real exposure is Farewell-class artifact/enchantment mass removal taking the Mine layer, the punishers, and the Reservoir in one card. Deploy in layers, never present both punishers plus the Reservoir to one board state, and keep the kill pieces in hand until the commit turn (strategy:pivot-point). Enlightened Tutor makes that discipline nearly free — the piece you have not fetched yet is un-sweepable, sitting in the library until the end step you schedule it. Loran of the Third Path plus a Displacer Kitten blink is your repeatable answer posture, and the Kitten ledger is honest: stack 005 refuted the mana-positive version — the loop is exactly mana-neutral with a one-time 3-mana exit.

Stax and tax: taxes attack your velocity math — many cheap spells per turn — so recount the hand under the tax before sequencing (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial). The kill's requirements are brutally small — the four pieces and {2} to start (stack 006) — so you RACE soft locks that don't touch artifact casts, and Enlightened Tutor finds the missing piece through a resource-starved board for one white mana. But cast-limit and cast-tax pieces beat the line structurally, not interactively: Rule of Law-class effects cap a 15-cast turn dead, and a per-spell tax breaks the 004-verified mana-neutrality. Against those your role flips to beatdown on the lock itself — answer the compounding second piece, not the first inconvenience. A lone Thalia is an annoyance; Thalia plus Deafening Silence is a funeral.

Teferi, Hero of Dominaria is this matchup's workhorse: the -3 is repeatable removal that TUCKS a lock piece — indestructibility and totem armor are irrelevant to third-from-the-top — and the +1's untap claws back mana under a Winter Orb-class effect. You are also partly the denial player yourself: Drannith Magistrate shuts off every opponent's commander and every non-hand cast, which in commander-dependent pods makes YOU the lock. Heliod's per-opponent-draw discount is the tax rebate no other deck gets — Kwain activations and The Second Doctor's end-step gifts keep growing it even under a Sphere — and Kitten-blinking Loran is repeatable lock-piece removal.

Aggro: Propaganda and The Second Doctor's no-attack rider are virtual card advantage tripled at a four-player table (strategy:card-advantage.virtual). Be honest about the wall count: Propaganda is your ONE maindeck attack tax — Ghostly Prison sits in the sideboard — and Archmage's Charm holds the slot a second tax could occupy, the bet that never-dead interaction beats a surcharge. Against aggro the Charm earns its keep anyway: counter the overrun or pump effect, or draw two when the coast is clear. Lean on the rider — the opponent who accepts the Doctor's card cannot attack you next turn — and on the punisher clock making you the worst-value attack at the table. Commit nothing, hold Supreme Verdict, and let them overextend into the uncounterable reset (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math).

The Fruition trap has a name: never lead Forced Fruition into an aggro pod. Sequence Iron Maiden or Ebony Owl Netsuke first so the seven-card refill arrives taxed (stack 003: hands over seven pay on upkeep, cleanup trims to exactly seven, damage lands before the cards are spent).

The life-ledger caveat this matchup owns: the Reservoir kill pays 50 life three times, and stack 006's 15-cast minimum is computed FROM 32 LIFE. The arithmetic generalizes — k(k+1)/2 must reach 151 minus your life total — so at 20 life the minimum is 16 casts, and at 8 life it is 17. Each extra cast is another open priority window, which means every point of chip damage you absorb is combo disruption whether the aggro player knows it or not. Your life total is a combo resource: pillow hard, let Kwain and the Reservoir's own setup-cast triggers pad the ledger, and go a turn earlier rather than a window longer.

Combo and storm: the discipline test, and you are built to pass it. The counter suite — Fierce Guardianship, Force of Negation, Swan Song, An Offer You Can't Refuse, Dovin's Veto, and Archmage's Charm — is held by turn 6 in 67.2% of goldfish games (78.1% ever). Spend it only on the card that ends the game, per the answer-economy bar (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy). Drannith Magistrate blanks commander-centric and non-hand lines before they start — flashback, escape, and cast-from-exile engines all die to 'from anywhere other than their hands' — so land it EARLY against a known combo seat and let it eat a removal spell that was earmarked for your win.

Enlightened Tutor resolves this matchup's oldest tension — hold interaction or assemble? — by doing both. It is an instant: tutor on an end step with counter mana already open, and the kill assembles end-of-turn before your untap. With wincon access at 50.5% by turn 6 (61.2% ever) and a verified 15-cast kill behind Grand Abolisher's closed windows, you are frequently the faster, better-protected combo deck in the pod. That flips your role to beatdown, and the racer does not durdle (strategy:whos-the-beatdown, strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window). One warning: the hug layer is a liability here. Kwain stays untapped, The Second Doctor's offer goes to the other two seats, and Forced Fruition stays in hand against spellslinger unless a punisher is down and you are the one about to win.

Graveyard decks and incidental hate: your own graveyard needs are trivial — Dig Through Time's delve and Torrential Gearhulk's flashback target — so an opposing Rest in Peace costs you a card's worth of value, not a plan, and it never touches the Hullbreaker kill. Against the graveyard seat, Drannith Magistrate is your real card: it stops every CAST from a graveyard (flashback, escape, disturb), though not reanimation — Reanimate-style effects put the creature onto the battlefield without casting it, and Drannith's text only polices casting. Know that distinction before you tap out trusting it. Against cast-based recursion Drannith is a lock piece; against true reanimator your answers are the counterspell suite and Path/Swords on the body — and that seat meets the free-counter bar early and often.
how_it_wins:
You're running the friendliest crime in the format: hand the whole table a firehose of cards, then charge for the water. Howling Mine, Font of Mythos, Temple Bell, Dictate of Kruphix, Kami of the Crescent Moon, Folio of Fancies, and the big one — Forced Fruition — all read symmetric, and Kwain and The Second Doctor make the generosity look sincere. Heliod is the hinge. The front face rebuys an enchantment on arrival; the {3}{U/P} flip into the Warped Eclipse grants everything flash and discounts your spells {1} for each card your opponents drew this turn. Every card the table accepts pays your mana bill on the turn you want to act.

The numbers back the patience. The goldfish sim has Heliod down by turn 6 in 90.2% of games (median turn 4). While the pieces gather, you play draw-go behind a counter suite held by turn 6 in 67.2% of games, with Supreme Verdict as the uncounterable reset your own planeswalkers survive.

Your primary win is verified end to end, and it is a storm kill: Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring + Arcane Signet + Aetherflux Reservoir (stack 006, checker-passed). The loop — each rock's cast bounces the other, tapped for its mana before it leaves — is exactly mana-neutral (stack 004), so casts are unbounded in one main phase. The Reservoir converts the count into life: cast n nets +n, so k casts pay out k(k+1)/2. From 32 life you need that sum to reach 119, which makes 15 casts the proven minimum — 14 casts pay only 105 and fail.

The verified schedule reads like a heist ledger. Casts 1–6 lift you to 53; the first 'Pay 50 life: 50 damage' activation drops you to 3 and kills the 26-life opponent via state-based actions. Casts 7–12 rebuild to 60; the second activation (60 to 10) kills the 40-life seat. Casts 13–15 reach 52; the third (52 to 2) takes the last, and with every opponent gone you win on the spot — one main phase, ending at 2 life.

The same artifact names the weakness, so respect it. Every activation and every loop cast opens a fully open priority window: activating an ability is not casting a spell, so Hullbreaker never triggers in those windows, and the sorcery-speed loop pieces can't respond to anything. Grand Abolisher is the named answer — during your turn, opponents can't cast spells or activate artifact, creature, or enchantment abilities. He closes exactly the windows the kill opens. Win-condition access is drawn by turn 6 in 50.5% of goldfish runs (61.2% of games ever), and the whole line needs {2} and the pieces, nothing more.

Path two is the clean one: Approach of the Second Sun. The first cast gains 7 life — 14 with Alhammarret's Archive out — and buries the card seventh from the top, trivially shallow when everyone draws in bulk and two doublers accelerate your digging. Mystical Tutor or Long-Term Plans puts it back on top directly. Stack 002 verified the second cast end to end: the win is checked during resolution, as a spell effect, and the first casting still counts because the game tracks the casting event, not the shuffled-away card. Their one and only window is while the second Approach sits on the stack — commit behind held countermagic, and once resolution begins, nothing stops it.

Path three is attrition, and it runs while you sleep. Iron Maiden and Viseling deal upkeep damage equal to hand size minus 4; Ebony Owl Netsuke deals a flat 4 at seven-plus cards. Stack 003 verified the arithmetic: Forced Fruition fills a hand, cleanup trims it to exactly 7, and next upkeep the Owl hits for 4 and the Maiden for 3 — 7 damage without you tapping a land, running on all three opponents' upkeeps. The Second Doctor makes 7 the floor, not the ceiling: no maximum hand size means the trim never happens, so a ten-card hand takes 6 from the Maiden while the Owl keeps firing. The engine-plus-punisher two-piece assembles by turn 6 in 41.2% of games, so most games open as pure control — the deck is built to be great at exactly that — and the moment the four kill pieces line up behind an Abolisher, you stop playing fair.

combo_lines.001: The question presented: is Hullbreaker Horror plus Sol Ring the two-card infinite 296,000 decklists say it is? The dispositive fact is targeting law. The Horror's trigger is modal, and mode and target lock in while the Sol Ring that caused it is still a spell on the stack — and a spell you control is neither 'target spell you don't control' nor a nonland permanent. By the time Sol Ring is a permanent, the trigger is gone. Holding: the pair alone loops nothing — no mana, no storm count. Never pitch this deck to the table, or compute its bracket, on the strength of that database line.
combo_lines.002: On the second Approach of the Second Sun, two questions decide games, and both resolve in your favor. First: the initial casting still counts even though the card was shuffled back into your library — the condition reads an event in the game's history, not the card object. Second: the win is checked mid-resolution, as a spell effect, not a state-based action. The opponents' one and only window is while Approach sits on the stack; the walk plays out the counter-war, including Swan Song answering their counterspell with {U} held. The holding anyone can carry to a table: once all players pass and resolution begins, the game simply ends.
combo_lines.003: Exhibit: an opponent Naturalizes Forced Fruition. The trigger sits on top of the very spell that caused it, so they draw their seven cards before the enchantment dies — and the ability would survive its source's destruction anyway. Cleanup then trims them to exactly 7 in hand, which is precisely the threshold both punishers want. Next upkeep, Ebony Owl Netsuke's intervening-if sees seven cards and deals 4; Iron Maiden deals 7 minus 4 = 3; 7 total. Both triggers are yours, so you order them — though here neither changes hand size, and the math is order-proof. Removal does not save them from the draws already owed.
combo_lines.004: The real Hullbreaker engine, entered into the record: three cards, not two. Cast the two-mana rock; the Horror's trigger targets Sol Ring, which IS a legal target now — a permanent on the battlefield, not a spell. Tap Sol Ring for {C}{C} while the trigger is pending (a mana ability; nothing responds), let the bounce resolve, recast Sol Ring, then bounce and tap the Signet in turn. One full cycle: 3 mana spent, 3 produced — exactly mana-neutral, so the cast count is unbounded within one main phase off a {2} investment. Two limits ride with the holding: the loop nets no mana, cards, or damage by itself, and aiming a trigger at an opponent's permanent breaks the chain. Thought Vessel substitutes for Arcane Signet exactly; Fellwar Stone, in the sideboard, sustains the cycle only while an opponent's land can actually produce mana.
combo_lines.005: The petition: Displacer Kitten blinks Sol Ring untapped mid-loop, and stack 004's mana-neutral cycle goes mana-positive. Denied. Both of your triggers lock their targets at announcement, and whichever resolves first turns the shared target into a new object — the second trigger's target is illegal, and it fizzles. Horror's bounce and the Kitten's blink are mutually exclusive on every cast. Keep the loop alive and the Kitten contributes exactly nothing: the cycle stays exactly 3 spent, 3 produced. Blink first and you really do tap Sol Ring twice on that cast — but the bounce fizzles, your hand empties, and the loop TERMINATES: a one-time exit worth 3 floating mana against the best Kitten-less exit's 2. Unbounded casts survive untouched; unbounded mana does not exist, and an X spell off this engine is capped at that terminal float of at most 3.
combo_lines.006: The verified table-kill, checker-passed end to end with an exact ledger, and the reason this deck's bracket-4 floor is honest: Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring + Arcane Signet + Aetherflux Reservoir. The 004-verified loop supplies unbounded casts; the Reservoir converts them — cast n nets +n life, so k casts pay k(k+1)/2, and from 32 life you need at least 119, making 15 casts the proven minimum (14 pays 105 and falls short). The walk interleaves three 'Pay 50 life' activations at the only legal points: 53 to 3 (first kill), 60 to 10 (second), 52 to 2 (third), each 50 damage killing its target via state-based actions, all in one main phase, you alive at 2. The verified weakness comes with the verdict: every activation opens a fully open priority window — activating is not casting, so Hullbreaker never triggers on it, and the sorcery-speed loop pieces can't be cast in response to anything. Grand Abolisher is the named answer: on your turn, his static closes every one of those windows.

card_roles.Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the: Front face: a 4/4 that returns a non-God enchantment from your graveyard on arrival — Forced Fruition or Rhystic Study back after a wrath is the usual pick. The {3}{U/P} flip (sorcery speed, payable with 2 life) turns on the deck: the Warped Eclipse grants your spells flash and discounts them {1} per card your opponents drew this turn. Your own table-draw engines, Kwain activations, and Second Doctor end-step gifts pay your costs while you keep mana up for counters.
card_roles.Forced Fruition: The punisher core's detonator: every opponent spell is seven forced draws, feeding Iron Maiden, Ebony Owl Netsuke, and Viseling past their thresholds instantly. Stack 003 verified the trigger resolves even when the spell it triggered on is the removal that kills it.
card_roles.Iron Maiden: Hand-size-minus-4 damage at each opponent's upkeep, computed on resolution. Inert against a five-card hand; a three-a-turn clock once the engines are running — and with The Second Doctor removing the cleanup trim, the count climbs past stack 003's floor of 3.
card_roles.Ebony Owl Netsuke: A flat 4 at each opponent's upkeep at seven-plus cards — the intervening-if is checked both at trigger and on resolution. With Iron Maiden, exactly 7 damage per punished upkeep off a cleanup-trimmed hand (stack 003); with The Second Doctor keeping hands untrimmed, the check just keeps passing.
card_roles.Viseling: Iron Maiden with a body — same hand-minus-4 upkeep damage on a 1/1 construct. Redundancy for the deck's core clock; dies to creature removal (and your own Supreme Verdict) where the Maiden doesn't.
card_roles.Kwain, Itinerant Meddler: The political engine: {T} lets each player draw, and drawers gain 1 life. Every card an opponent accepts inches them toward the punisher thresholds and grows Heliod's discount; every card they decline is a card behind. Your side of the tap doubles twice under Alhammarret's Archive — two cards and 2 life. A two-mana body that makes the whole table like you buys exactly the waiting turns a 41.2%-by-turn-6 two-piece needs.
card_roles.The Second Doctor: 'Players have no maximum hand size' is the quiet punisher enabler: opponents never trim at cleanup, so Ebony Owl's 7+ check keeps passing and Iron Maiden's hand-minus-4 grows unbounded — while you hoard your own doubled draws behind Thought Vessel's no-maximum clause. The end-step rider is a pillow fort on legs: each opponent who accepts the draw can't attack you or your permanents next turn, stacking with Propaganda — and the cards they take feed the Maiden anyway. Heads they can't attack, tails they fall behind.
card_roles.Alhammarret's Archive: The asymmetry hinge for both of the deck's currencies: every draw of yours after the first in your draw step becomes two, and all your lifegain doubles. Kwain's tap pays you double on both halves, the Mine effects become personal Fonts on your side only, a first Approach of the Second Sun banks 14 life instead of 7, and it stacks with Teferi's Ageless Insight as a second your-side draw doubler. Five mana that converts every symmetric engine you run into a rigged one.
card_roles.Supreme Verdict: The uncounterable reset: four mana, destroy all creatures, and the blue player can do nothing about it. Your clock lives in artifacts and enchantments, so the wrath is nearly one-sided — it does take Kwain, Kami, and your other engine bodies, so time it for when the board, not your own value layer, is the problem.
card_roles.Psychosis Crawler: Drains each opponent for 1 per card YOU draw, and its stats track your hand. With the X-draw suite and the doublers it converts a big refill into table-wide reach — a candidate line flagged for stack verification, not yet walked.
card_roles.Scrawling Crawler: A symmetric upkeep draw stapled to an asymmetric tax: each opponent draw costs them a life, so every engine on your board turns it into a slow burn.
card_roles.Sphinx's Tutelage: Turns your own draws into repeated two-card mills with a shared-color cascade — an alternate attrition angle that scales with the draw doublers and the wheels.
card_roles.Howling Mine: The classic symmetric engine: an extra draw at each draw step while untapped. Symmetric on its face; the punishers, the Archive, and Heliod's discount make it yours.
card_roles.Font of Mythos: Howling Mine doubled — two extra draws for everyone. The fastest way to push the table to seven cards, and the biggest per-turn Heliod discount.
card_roles.Temple Bell: A draw for everyone on demand, at instant speed — which means you can ring it on an opponent's upkeep after their draw step to push a hand over the punisher threshold, or in response to removal for pure value.
card_roles.Dictate of Kruphix: The flash Howling Mine — deploy it end of turn, ahead of the opponent whose upkeep you most want taxed.
card_roles.Kami of the Crescent Moon: Howling Mine on legs for two mana. Cheapest engine in the deck; also the most fragile.
card_roles.Folio of Fancies: Three jobs: removes YOUR maximum hand size, force-feeds the table X cards at once, and can mill an opponent for their whole (bloated) hand. The X-draw activation is the precision tool for pushing hands over 7 at the right moment.
card_roles.Rhystic Study: The asymmetric half of the value layer: every opponent spell is a card or a tax, and in a deck this dense with forced action it is a firehose. The Warped Eclipse doesn't discount off it (it counts draws, and Study's draws are yours) — but it wins the card war that decides control mirrors.
card_roles.Mystic Remora: Rhystic Study's early-game twin — a turn-1 Remora often draws three-plus cards before the cumulative upkeep bites. Pay a couple of ages, then let it go — or don't: a Displacer Kitten blink returns it as a new object with no age counters, and the tax restarts from zero.
card_roles.Smothering Tithe: Every opponent draw is {2} or a Treasure for you — and this deck makes opponents draw in sevens. Forced Fruition plus Tithe presents seven pay-or-treasure decisions per opponent spell (flagged for stack verification of the exact yield).
card_roles.Consecrated Sphinx: Two cards to you for every card an opponent draws. Under any table engine this is obscene; under Forced Fruition it is fourteen cards per opponent spell. The single strongest magnet for removal you play.
card_roles.Teferi's Ageless Insight: Doubles every draw of yours past the first each draw step — your Howling Mines become personal Fonts, and digging seven cards to a buried Approach takes half the turns. Stacks with Alhammarret's Archive.
card_roles.Faerie Mastermind: Flash body that pays you a card whenever an opponent draws their second card each turn — free value under your own engines — with an activated Temple Bell stapled on for pushing hands at instant speed.
card_roles.Hullbreaker Horror: The spine of the verified primary win. An uncounterable flash 7/8 whose cast trigger bounces a spell or permanent — a tempo monster in the midgame, and with Sol Ring plus Arcane Signet it is the unbounded, mana-neutral cast loop (stack 004) that Aetherflux Reservoir converts into the table-kill (stack 006). Two verified limits: the two-card 'infinite' with Sol Ring alone is refuted (stack 001), and the Horror gives the kill zero protection — activating the Reservoir is not casting, so its trigger never fires during the windows that matter.
card_roles.Displacer Kitten: Blinks one of your nonland permanents on each noncreature cast — and in a 99 that is mostly noncreature spells, that is constantly. The oracle-grounded payoffs: a blinked Mystic Remora returns as a new object with zero age counters, so the cumulative upkeep resets (the long-run value of that free Remora is still a candidate line, not yet walked); a blinked tapped Sol Ring returns untapped; a blinked Loran or Faerie Mastermind re-triggers and untaps for another activation. One question is settled, and the answer is no: stack 005 refutes the hope that the Kitten makes the stack-004 loop mana-positive. Target lock at announcement plus the new-object rule make its blink and Horror's bounce mutually exclusive on every cast, so the loop stays exactly mana-neutral, and blinking Sol Ring is a one-time, loop-terminating exit worth +1 floating mana.
card_roles.Sol Ring: The best rock in the format and one of the four pieces of the verified kill — the loop taps it for {C}{C} with the bounce trigger already on the stack (stack 004), and every recast adds one to the Reservoir's count (stack 006).
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Fixes into either color and completes the kill engine: its cast bounces Sol Ring, its tap keeps the cycle at exactly 3-in, 3-out (stack 004) — and in stack 006's walk it is cast #1 of the fifteen.
card_roles.Thought Vessel: Two jobs verified or textual: an exact substitute for Arcane Signet in the Hullbreaker loop (same neutral ledger, per stack 004), and no-maximum-hand-size insurance that survives the creature wraths The Second Doctor doesn't.
card_roles.Fierce Guardianship: Free countermagic while Heliod is out — the card that lets you tap out for an engine piece and still say no. Part of why the sim shows interaction held by turn 6 in 67.2% of games.
card_roles.Force of Negation: The other free counter: pitch a blue card on an opponent's turn to stop a noncreature spell and exile it. Guards the punisher board through your tapped-out turns.
card_roles.Swan Song: One mana, counters the counterspell aimed at your second Approach — the exact play walked in stack 002. The 2/2 Bird is a bargain against winning the game.
card_roles.An Offer You Can't Refuse: One-mana noncreature counter; the two Treasures you hand over are a real cost, so aim it at spells that matter — sweepers, counters in the Approach war.
card_roles.Dovin's Veto: The argument-ender: can't be countered itself. The premium hold for your commit turn.
card_roles.Counterspell: The unconditional classic. Two blue is easy off 26 blue land sources, 31 counting the rocks.
card_roles.Arcane Denial: Counters anything for {1}{U} and replaces itself next upkeep; the two cards it feeds the opponent are, in this deck, more fuel for your punishers.
card_roles.Approach of the Second Sun: The clean second wincon. First cast: 7 life — 14 under Alhammarret's Archive — and seventh from the top, shallow when everyone's drawing in bulk. Second cast from hand wins during resolution, verified end to end in stack 002; the only window to stop it is on the stack. Wincon access sits at 50.5% by turn 6 in the goldfish, so between this and the storm kill the tutors always have a live target.
card_roles.Aetherflux Reservoir: The verified kill (stack 006). 'Gain 1 life for each spell you've cast this turn' turns the mana-neutral Hullbreaker loop into triangular life growth — cast n nets +n — and three 'Pay 50 life: 50 damage' activations clear the table in one main phase, 15 casts minimum from 32 life. Remember the verified fine print: the 50 life is paid before anyone can respond, and each activation's window is fully open unless Grand Abolisher is down.
card_roles.Metallurgic Summonings: Constructs sized to each instant or sorcery you cast; the buyback clause returns your whole spell graveyard once you control six artifacts, which this deck reaches without trying.
card_roles.Mystical Tutor: The Approach enabler: end-step tutor puts the second copy on top for the win next turn (stack 002's setup). Also finds Supreme Verdict or the right counterspell on demand — part of why wincon access sits at 50.5% by turn 6.
card_roles.Long-Term Plans: Any card, third from the top — with your draw density and two doublers that's one turn away. Unlike Mystical Tutor it can fetch permanents: Aetherflux, a punisher, the missing loop rock.
card_roles.Mathemagics: Draws 2^X cards — the most explosive refill in the deck and the scariest thing to point at yourself with Psychosis Crawler out (candidate line, unverified).
card_roles.Prosperity: Symmetric X-draw for the table: pushes every hand toward punisher range at once, on your terms.
card_roles.Skyscribing: Prosperity with a forecast rider — a free-ish draw for everyone each upkeep from your hand, keeping hands topped up without spending the card.
card_roles.Braingeyser: Targeted X-draw: refill yourself, or force-feed one opponent over the Netsuke threshold at sorcery speed.
card_roles.Stroke of Genius: Braingeyser at instant speed — refill on an end step, or push a hand over 7 in response to their upkeep triggers going on the stack.
card_roles.Dig Through Time: Delve makes this two mana in the mid game: seven deep for exactly the two cards you need — usually a counter and a threat, or the buried Approach.
card_roles.Propaganda: The standing attack tax: attackers cost {2} each, and with The Second Doctor's no-attack rider and punisher upkeep damage on top, attacking you is the worst-value line at the table. The honest count: this is your one maindeck tax — Ghostly Prison sits in the sideboard — the bet that never-dead interaction beats a redundant tax at a draw-go table.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: The panic button: life locked, everything phases out, you lose nothing to the wrath — and your engine board returns intact before your untap.
card_roles.Cyclonic Rift: The asymmetric reset. Overloaded on an end step it clears every opposing board while your punisher artifacts stay put.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: Premium one-mana creature exile; the life you give away comes back as upkeep damage.
card_roles.Path to Exile: The second one-mana exile. The basic land you gift is a real cost — save it for the creature that actually kills you.
card_roles.Loran of the Third Path: Artifact/enchantment removal on a body, plus a tap that draws you and an opponent a card — removal that also feeds the punishers, and the premium Displacer Kitten blink target for a re-triggered Disenchant.
card_roles.Torrential Gearhulk: Flash 5/6 that recasts a counterspell or Dig Through Time from the graveyard for free — a threat that interacts the turn it arrives.
card_roles.Leyline of Anticipation: Flash for everything before Heliod flips (and redundancy after) — free from the opening hand, which is when the deck most wants to play draw-go.
card_roles.Temple of Enlightenment: Enters tapped and scries 1 on the way in — a free look and a bottomed blank on exactly the turns you weren't holding up interaction anyway. After that it taps for white or blue every turn for the rest of the game, which is what a base carrying a {U}{U}{U} card and a {1}{W}{W}{U} wrath needs from every dual it plays.
card_roles.Mikokoro, Center of the Sea: A Temple Bell on a land: repeatable, uncounterable hand-stuffing that survives every board wipe.
card_roles.Irrigated Farmland: Taps for either colour, enters tapped, and — the clause you actually keep it for — cycles for {2}. Flooding out is the one way a draw-go deck beats itself, and this is the land that refuses to be the draw that isn't a spell. Make your drops early with it; turn it into a card once you don't need the drop.
card_roles.Grand Abolisher: The kill-turn shield for exactly the hole stack 006 verifies: every Reservoir activation and every loop cast opens a fully open priority window, Hullbreaker offers no protection (activating isn't casting), and the sorcery-speed pieces can't respond to anything. Abolisher's static — during your turn, opponents can't cast spells or activate abilities of artifacts, creatures, or enchantments — closes every one of those windows. Lead the commit turn with him; two mana buys an uninterruptable 15-cast line.
card_roles.Drannith Magistrate: One of the ten Game Changers on the bracket report, and a denial engine in one static: opponents can't cast spells from anywhere but their hands — no commanders from the command zone, no flashback, no foretell, no cascade. In commander-dependent pods you are suddenly the lock. The stranding package with Supreme Verdict or Path (exile the commander, Drannith locks the recast) is a flagged candidate line, not yet stack-verified.
card_roles.Jace Beleren: A Howling Mine that survives Farewell — and your own Supreme Verdict. The +2 hands every player a card, feeding the punisher thresholds and Heliod's discount from three opponents at once while ticking toward more loyalty; the −1 pushes a specific hand over the Netsuke line, or draws you the piece. Three mana for a table engine no wrath in the format's mainstream removal suite touches.
card_roles.Jace, Wielder of Mysteries: A standing wincon in a permanent: 'If you would draw a card while your library has no cards in it, you win the game instead,' with a +1 that draws while it threatens. It's part of why goldfish wincon access sits at 50.5% by turn 6. The deliberate self-deck win — Archive-doubled X-draws emptying your own library — is a flagged candidate awaiting a stack scenario; the replacement-ordering questions are real, so don't bet the game on it until it's walked.
card_roles.Teferi, Temporal Pilgrim: The planeswalker built for a deck that does nothing but draw: every draw adds loyalty, so under your Mine effects and doublers he charges himself faster than the table can attack him down — and he survives your own Supreme Verdict. The −2 Spirit grows a +1/+1 counter per draw into a real blocker-then-threat, and the −12 is a one-sided board shuffle you actually reach.
card_roles.Teferi, Hero of Dominaria: The fourth sweep-surviving walker, and the one built for this deck's exact posture: the +1 draws a card and untaps up to two lands at the next end step, so the clock advances while your Counterspell mana stays open — he survives every Supreme Verdict, including yours. The −3 tucks any nonland permanent third from the top, your only repeatable answer to a resolved artifact or enchantment besides Cyclonic Rift, and the −8 emblem — exile a permanent per draw — ends the game in a deck that does nothing but draw.
card_roles.Archmage's Charm: Interaction that is never dead: counter a spell, draw two at an end step under Heliod's discount, or take a nonland permanent with mana value 1 or less — an opposing Sol Ring at a rock-heavy bracket-4 table. The honest cost is the deck's only {U}{U}{U}: Karsten's table wants 37 blue sources for a triple pip on curve and this base targets 36, so treat it as a turn-4-plus spell cast off duals and the discount, not a turn-3 promise.
card_roles.Enlightened Tutor: The consistency engine and the tenth Game Changer: one white mana, at instant speed, puts any artifact or enchantment on top of your library — Aetherflux Reservoir, the missing loop rock (Sol Ring, Arcane Signet, or the substitute Thought Vessel), a punisher (Iron Maiden, Ebony Owl Netsuke, Forced Fruition itself), or a value engine like Rhystic Study or Smothering Tithe. It reaches every piece of the verified kill except Hullbreaker Horror, the one creature — cast on the end step before your commit turn, it converts a three-of-four board into a scheduled four-of-four. Honest fine print: it tops, not draws, so the piece arrives a draw step later unless a Mine effect picks it up — which this deck of Howling Mines usually provides.

mulligan:
The sim keeps 73.8% of first sevens and mulligans gently — 0.33 per game — so the bar is simple. Two to four lands, one card-flow piece, and something that says no. Kept hands center on 2-3 lands plus rocks: at 33 lands your drops take care of themselves, so the rocks are buying turns rather than covering a shortfall, and Ancient Tomb plus a two-drop rock is how 27.7% of games cast Heliod by turn 3.

You're mulliganing toward flow plus interaction, not toward any combo. A table-draw engine is drawn by turn 6 in 75.4% of games (mean turn 2.5) — call it the 75% promise. Cheap or free interaction is held by then in 67.2% (78.1% of games ever). Those are your reliable axes, and Kwain and Jace Beleren both count among the cheap engines worth keeping a hand for.

The trap has a name: the two-piece. Engine PLUS punisher assembles by turn 6 in only 41.2% of games (56.7% ever, mean turn 4.2), so never keep a marginal hand because it 'promises the lock.' The punishers are inert on their own — Iron Maiden reads hand minus 4, and against a normal hand that's one damage. A hand of two punishers and no draw engine is a mulligan in costume. Ship it.

The same discipline applies doubly to the verified kill: four specific pieces is not a mulligan target. It's what Long-Term Plans and the 75.4% draw engine find for you in the midgame. And don't dig for wincons at hand-quality prices — access is 50.5% by turn 6 with Jace, Wielder of Mysteries counting as a standing wincon, and the tutors carry the rest.

Heliod himself needs no help: 90.2% of games cast him by turn 6, median turn 4. Keep hands that use the turns before him — Remora into rock into Kami (or Kwain) is the curve this deck was built to play.
upgrades:
The Short List is ten names — seven from the 61-card bench, three scouted from the wider pool — and the pruning did the real work. Spare lands, one-shot cantrip bodies, fair stunners, and token boards that walk into your own Supreme Verdict all fail the same test: an engine deck at a tier-4 table doesn't sleeve cards that feed no verified line. What survives is whatever makes the proven machines better — the Reservoir kill, the Approach plan B, the punisher clock. Six checker-passed stacks and a 10,000-game goldfish log are the filter; taste never got a vote.

The top of the list buys certainty where the ledgers already point. Mana Vault leads: the loop is verified mana-neutral and its mana-positive extension is refuted, so a rock that casts for {1} and taps for {C}{C}{C} is the one candidate that flips the sign — every recast another Reservoir trigger toward the lethal. Teferi, Time Raveler is the redundancy the shield lacks: Grand Abolisher has no backup, and a static that holds opponents to sorcery speed covers the whole go-turn — and survives the creature sweepers a two-mana body doesn't.

Two entries carry their own conditions, and the conditions are the point. Sphinx of the Final Word comes in at two or more heavy-permission seats — its static makes the second Approach cast counter-proof, though it is no Abolisher substitute, since a Reservoir activation is not a cast. No More Lies comes in at fast-combo pods, where the slowest symmetric engine is pure fuel for the storm seat. Read each entry's condition before you shop: on this list, when is as load-bearing as what.
mana_base:
Thirty-three lands, spread over 18 entries, and seven of them enter tapped. That is 21% — inside the one-in-three budget, and softer than the number reads. Only Temple of Enlightenment and Irrigated Farmland come down tapped unconditionally. Glacial Fortress asks for a Plains or an Island against 17 basics, Prairie Stream for two basics, Deserted Beach and Seachrome Coast for a land count you cross going either direction, and Hallowed Fountain just takes 2 life.

The colour split is the story, and it is a story about matching work to sources. Blue does 79.2% of the pip labour — 61 pips across 40 cards — on 63.4% of the land sources. White does 20.8%, 16 pips across 14 cards, on 36.6%. White still runs ahead of its pip load, but it isn't taking that from blue: 11 of the 15 white sources tap for blue as well. Three Plains and Eiganjo are the only white-only mana in the deck.

On curve, lands alone, you make white 78.7% of the time and blue 74.2%. Rocks and dorks lift those to 88.1% and 83.9%. The 90% yardstick asks for 36 blue sources and 22 white; you run 26 and 15 in lands, 31 and 20 with the rocks counted. The audit says it plainly — that target is a yardstick, not a possibility, in a 33-land deck — and the two colours now miss it by shares that track the work each one does.

Six rocks, one ritual and three cost-reducers close the rest. Arcane Signet, Azorius Signet and Talisman of Progress each add either colour on demand; Sol Ring and Thought Vessel pay generic freight only; Smothering Tithe turns opposing draws into Treasures of any colour, and this deck makes opponents draw in sevens. Watch the handoff in the goldfish. The land-drop hit rate slides from 86.6% on turn 3 to 72.5% on turn 4 to 47.1% by turn 6, while mean available mana keeps climbing: 4.12 on four, 5.325 on six, 7.033 by ten. That is the rocks and the fetch taking over from the draws.

One last reason the yardstick reads harsh here: it prices every on-curve cast at sticker, and this deck rarely pays sticker. The Warped Eclipse shaves {1} per card your opponents drew this turn, and a discount only ever eats generic mana. Pips never get cheaper. Blue's effective pip load of 2, with a maximum of 3, is the number to plan around — Archmage's Charm's {U}{U}{U} is a cast you set up off duals, not a turn-three promise.
